newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN INSTABILITY WORRIES FOREIGN INVESTORS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN INSTABILITY WORRIES FOREIGN INVESTORS.

text.p: Bulgaria needs to resolve its political crisis quickly as its crumbling economy cannot accomodate reform delays, foreign investors said on Tuesday.

"The political crisis has to come to an end as soon as possible in order to secure a more attractive environment to investors," said Christos Katsanis, chairman of the Bulgarian International Business Association, which groups major foreign investors.

Bulgarian President Zhelyu Zhelev has declined to invite the Socialists' prime minister-designate Nikolai Dobrev to form a new cabinet to replace the Socialist government of Zhan Videnov, who resigned as prime minister on December 21.

The Socialists have agreed to hold talks with the opposition on their demand for a general election but want to propose a government with a programme for 500 days, about the length of mandate remaining to the present parliament.
"Bulgaria cannot recover its ailing economy without first guaranteeing political stability, otherwise it is like putting the cart before the horse," said one foreign investor.
Bulgaria's political showdown between the ruling Socialist Party and the opposition brings closer the prospect of debt default and hyperinflation, analysts say.

Month-on-month inflation soared to 26.9 percent in December from just over nine percent in November after a series of price increases on basic food and fuel items. Annual inflation is running at a rate of more than 300 percent and the lev has fallen to 670 to the dollar now compared to 70 a year ago.

The International Monetary Fund had begun talks with the outgoing Socialist government, on the implementation of a strict fixed exchange rate regime as a last resort to stabilise the crumbling financial system.
The IMF said it is ready to complete talks on helping to haul Bulgaria's crumbling economy back from the brink of default as soon as it has a stable government.
Preparations for the currency board, due to be completed by February, included restructuring the central bank, passing in parliament a viable 1997 budget and approving amendments to banking laws.
Parliament, whose building suffered serious damage in a 10-hour demonstrators' siege on Friday, is being hurriedly repaired, so that plenary sessions can resume on Wednesday.
"Elections, which now seem inevitable must take place as soon as possible, to enable the new majority to begin everything from the beginning," said Katsanis.
